overview: Fluid reasoning is your ability to spot a pattern and work out its rule on the spot, without relying on words or facts you already know. In IQ tests it appears as number series, shape sequences and matrices where you must find what comes next. Regular practice helps you spot rules faster and check them more carefully.

strategy.b: Before you guess, check how each term relates to the one before it. Start with the simplest idea, such as adding a fixed number, then try multiplying. Only accept a rule once it fits every term given.

strategy.h: Test the rule on every term
strategy.b: A rule that fits the first two terms can fail on the third. Run your rule across the whole series before you commit to an answer. If it breaks, look for a second layer, such as steps that alternate.

When the terms do not multiply neatly, write the gaps between them underneath. The gaps may follow their own pattern, such as growing by one each time. A row of differences often reveals a rule the raw numbers hide.

Work out the missing term from your rule before you look at the options. If two choices look close, test both against every term. A rule you spot in twenty seconds is worth more than a long stare at the page.

drills.name: Number series
drills.how: Look at the gap between each pair of neighbouring terms to find what comes next. Say the rule in a short phrase, such as add 4 each time, before you check the options.
drills.tip: Write the gaps straight below the numbers so the pattern is visible.
drills.mistake: Testing the rule on the first two terms only, then getting caught out by the third. Check your rule across every term before picking an answer.

ex.why: Each term adds 4 to the one before (7 - 3 = 4, 11 - 7 = 4, 15 - 11 = 4), so the next term is 15 + 4 = 19.

drills.name: Growth series
drills.how: Spot the multiplying rule by dividing each term by the one before it. If the ratio stays the same, the series grows by a fixed multiple, such as doubling or tripling.
drills.tip: Try multiplying and dividing before you try adding, since many sequences grow by a factor.
drills.mistake: Assuming the series adds a fixed number when each term is really multiplied. Divide neighbouring terms to check, because a steady gap will not show a steady ratio.

ex.why: Each term is double the one before (10 = 5 x 2, 20 = 10 x 2, 40 = 20 x 2), so the next term is 40 x 2 = 80.

drills.name: Zig-zag series
drills.how: Look for two rules that alternate, so the series steps up one way and then the other. Split the terms into odd and even positions and check each group on its own.
drills.tip: Number the positions 1, 2, 3 and so on, then check which rule applies to each position.
drills.mistake: Using one rule for every step, which breaks the moment the pattern switches. Split the series into two interleaved lists and test each one separately.

ex.why: Terms in odd positions rise by 2 (2, 4, 6), while terms in even positions stay at 9, so the next term is 9.

drills.name: Widening gaps
drills.how: Write the gap between each pair of terms and see how those gaps change. When the gaps grow by a steady amount, predict the next gap and add it to the last term.
drills.tip: Work only with the gaps until you have found the next one, then add it to the last term.
drills.mistake: Adding the same gap every time even though the gap itself keeps increasing. Check whether the gaps form their own simple series.

ex.why: The gaps between terms are 1, 2, 3, 4, so the next gap is 5 and 11 + 5 = 16.

drills.name: Chain sums
drills.how: Each term is built from the two terms before it, often by adding them. Check the early terms by adding the pair before each one, then use the same sum to find the missing term.
drills.tip: Add the last two terms in your head and say the total aloud, which keeps the chain moving quickly.
drills.mistake: Adding the wrong pair, such as the term before last and the term two places back. Write out each pair so you always add the right two numbers.

ex.why: Each term is the sum of the two before it (2 = 1 + 1, 3 = 1 + 2, 5 = 2 + 3), so the next term is 3 + 5 = 8.

levels: Level 1: Single-step series of small numbers, such as adding the same amount each time, with about 30 seconds per question.
Level 2: Single-step series with slightly larger numbers and some subtracting, with about 25 seconds per question.
Level 3: Growth series where you must multiply or divide by a steady factor, with about 20 seconds per question.
Level 4: Zig-zag and widening-gap series that need two rules working together, with about 18 seconds per question.
Level 5: Chain sums and mixed series built from two-digit and three-digit numbers, with about 15 seconds per question.
Level 6: Long series that mix every rule type with large numbers, with about 12 seconds per question.
routine: Day 1: Do ten number series, saying the rule aloud before you check each answer.
Day 2: Solve ten growth series, dividing neighbouring terms to test for a steady ratio.
Day 3: Work through ten zig-zag or widening-gap series, writing the gaps underneath each one.
Day 4: Do ten chain sums against a timer, aiming for about 20 seconds each.
Day 5: Mix all five drill types into a timed set of 15, then review every miss.
